claims.text: Near-equiatomic five-transition-metal HENA nanoparticles exhibit suppressed atomic diffusion relative to traditional binary or ternary alloy nanoparticles at elevated temperatures.
Near-equiatomic five-transition-metal HENA nanoparticles have enhanced thermal stability relative to traditional binary or ternary alloy nanoparticles.
Severe lattice distortion suppresses atomic diffusion in these nanoparticles.
High configurational entropy stabilizes the solid-solution phase against phase separation.
The initial nanoparticles contain approximately 20 at% of each of five transition metals.
The initial nanoparticles have a single FCC or BCC solid-solution structure.
Atomic-size mismatch induces severe lattice distortion.
Severe lattice distortion increases the activation-energy barrier for atomic diffusion.
High configurational entropy increases the activation-energy barrier for atomic diffusion.
A sluggish-diffusion effect operates in the five-component nanoparticles.
Configurational-entropy stabilization raises the barrier for nucleation and growth of secondary phases.
Sluggish diffusion and configurational entropy retard phase separation and grain growth relative to traditional alloys.
The HENA nanoparticles will retain a single-phase solid solution after annealing.
The HENA nanoparticles will show minimal grain growth and no detectable phase separation after annealing.
Traditional binary or ternary comparator nanoparticles will undergo rapid phase separation, segregation, amorphization, or formation of distinct intermetallic compounds upon heating.
Below approximately 2 nm, surface energy may dominate bulk configurational entropy and invalidate the stability hypothesis.
Atomic-size mismatch above approximately 15% may cause immediate amorphization rather than formation of a stable solid solution.
The specific magnitude of sluggish diffusion in five-component nanoparticles and the proposed critical size threshold are not established by the supplied records.

contradictions.description: The comparator is variously described as a traditional alloy of similar composition, a binary or ternary alloy made from the same constituent elements, and a binary alloy of the same elements. A binary comparator cannot simultaneously contain the same five-component composition, so the control composition is internally ambiguous.
